title: Only 6% of Employees Turn to HR for Help. That's a Trust Problem, Not a Wellbeing Problem.
summary: Only 6% of Southeast Asian employees turn to HR for help. Why more wellbeing perks won't fix that, and what builds the trust that will.
body_markdown:
Most organisations in Southeast Asia have answered the wellbeing question the same way: by buying something. An employee assistance programme. A mental health app. Wellness days. Then they look at the usage numbers and wonder what went wrong.


A study of 6,000 employees across Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines offers a clue. Only 6% said they turn to HR for help.


One caveat before we go further: the study was co-created by Intellect, a mental health provider, with research firm Milieu Insight. Read its numbers on demand for wellbeing benefits with that in mind. The 6% figure is the one HR should lose sleep over, because no vendor has an interest in inflating it.


## Employees say they're fine. The data says otherwise.


In the same study, 72% of respondents rated their mental health as good or very good. Yet many also reported anxiety, exhaustion and feeling mentally disconnected, especially junior employees.


Other data points the same way:


- In the Philippines, 50% of employees experienced a lot of stress the previous day, according to Gallup. Jobstreet found only 41% of Filipino workers feel in control of their stress, and 38% feel burned out or extremely exhausted.
- In Singapore, 43% of employees reported daily stress.
- One in five employees across the region said they wouldn't consider a job without mental health support unless it was very well paid.
- In Thailand, 56% said they would take a pay cut for better wellbeing benefits.


The demand is real. The usage isn't. Even the study's authors note that stigma and poor integration mean benefits employees value often go unused.


## Why employees don't go to HR


Ask employees privately and the reasons are rarely about the quality of the support on offer. They're about who's offering it.


**HR is seen as the company's side.** The same team that handles wellbeing also handles appraisals, disciplinary cases and exits. Employees aren't confused about that.


**They fear it will go on record.** Admitting you're struggling feels risky when promotions and bonuses are on the line.


**Speaking up still carries a cost.** In many workplaces across the region, raising personal struggles with someone more senior is still seen as weakness or as burdening others.


**Nobody has told them what stays confidential.** Vague promises of "confidentiality" are not enough. People want to know exactly who will see what.


**The problem is their manager.** And their manager is often the gatekeeper to everything else.


It's telling that research cited by Harvard Business Review found 58% of employees feel safer talking to a bot than to their manager. That's not a compliment to bots. It's a warning about how safe people feel being honest with other people at work.


## What actually builds trust


**1. Be explicit about anonymity and confidentiality.** They're different. Anonymous means nobody knows who said it. Confidential means only named people can see it. Tell employees which channel is which, and who has access.


**2. Go to them instead of waiting.** A 6% walk-in rate means waiting for employees to come to HR doesn't work. Regular, short check-ins at key moments, such as after joining, after a manager change or after a tough quarter, bring problems to you.


**3. Act on what you hear, and say so.** Nothing builds trust faster than an employee raising something and seeing it change. Nothing destroys it faster than silence.


**4. Train managers as first responders, not counsellors.** Managers don't need to fix mental health. They need to notice, listen and point people to the right support without making it a performance conversation.


**5. Measure usage, not availability.** Track who actually uses support, by level, team and country. If junior employees aren't using it, ask why before you buy another programme.


**6. Put support where people already are.** Employees will talk on the chat apps they already use. Asking them to download yet another app is a barrier, not a benefit.


## The bottom line


Southeast Asian employees want wellbeing support. What most of them don't have is a channel they trust enough to use. Fixing that is less about buying more benefits and more about how HR listens, who can see what, and what happens after someone speaks up.
